question:
Client: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi. Matter: motor accident claim, death of spouse.

Her husband was killed in a road accident involving a commercial truck. The truck driver was operating the vehicle without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies the claim, arguing the policy is void because the driver was unlicensed, and that it bears no liability.

Key facts: deceased aged 42; monthly income Rs 35,000; dependants are the wife and two minor children (8 and 12); the truck was a commercial vehicle owned by a transport company; the driver held no valid licence; the insurer contests liability.

Research the corpus and advise on supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

17. The heading “Insurance of Motor Vehicles against Third Party Risks” given in Chapter XI of the

18. Reading the provisions of Sections 146 and 147 of the Motor Vehicles Act, it is evidently clear

payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Full Bench held that when a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
payload.ratio: Pursuant to the mandate of Section 149(1) and (4) of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment or award as a judgment debtor and recover the amount from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.

payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Court held that where a driving license is renewed more than 30 days after its expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period of the accident, but directed the insurance company to satisfy the award and recover the amount from the insured owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured. The breach must be conscious and wilful on the part of the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver held only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial). The court held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights against the owner/driver.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent. It squarely holds that even where the insurer proves a conscious breach (driver lacking proper licence for commercial vehicle), the third-party claimant is still entitled to payment from the insurer, who can then recover from the insured. This defeats the insurer's primary defence.
supporting.quote: Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings as the case may be, as ordered by the Claims Tribunal or the Court.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased was a third-party victim (cyclist) hit by a Mahindra Maxi Cab. The driver had an LMV licence but no commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable. Our case involves a commercial truck with a driver holding no licence at all — this is a stronger case for the claimant on the liability principle.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supreme Court authority that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties overrides contractual defences based on licence deficiencies. The Court emphasised that the third party's right to recover from the insurer is a statutory right that cannot be defeated by policy breaches.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment or award as a judgment debtor and recover the amount from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision holding that even fundamental breach does not absolve the insurer of liability to third parties. The only exception is fraud/collusion between the victim and insured — which is not alleged here.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench authority that comprehensively answers the insurer's argument. It holds that the 'pay and recover' principle applies irrespective of whether the policy is an Act policy or a contractual policy, and even for fundamental breaches.
supporting.quote: The Insurer is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149(2), even if it is a fundamental breach (that is breach of condition which is the cause for the accident) and the insurer proves the said breach, in view of the mandate under Section 149(1) of the Act.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, but to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all — identical to our facts. The Tribunal found a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant, citing Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba and Shamanna.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match in the corpus: a driver with no licence at all. Despite finding a fundamental breach, the Tribunal protected the third party by ordering pay-and-recover. This directly supports our client's position that she must be paid.
supporting.quote: It is admitted fact that the offending vehicle is covered with valid insurance at the time of alleged accident... the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence but no badge/authorisation for tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle). The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck with no licence at all — the principle applies a fortiori.
supporting.why_it_matters: Madras High Court confirms that even where the insurer proves breach, the proper remedy is pay-and-recover, not absolving the insurer. The court specifically held that 'the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation and recover it from the owner.'
supporting.quote: Keeping in view the nature of injuries... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent - Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV/transport endorsement but not HGV endorsement for a lorry (16,200 kg). The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our commercial truck case is analogous — the driver lacked the required licence for the vehicle class.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the driver is not licensed for the specific class of commercial vehicle, the third-party claimant is protected. The insurer must pay first and recover later.
supporting.quote: When the driver of the vehicle involved in the accident did not have a valid driving licence, whether the insurer can be directed to pay compensation to the Claimants and recover the same subsequently from the insured.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: The multiplier must be applied with reference to the age of the deceased, future prospects must be awarded even for self-employed persons based on standardised percentages, and appellate courts have power to enhance compensation.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 23, self-employed. The court applied Sarla Verma multiplier table (age-based), added future prospects, and corrected the Tribunal's errors. Our deceased is 42 — multiplier of 14 applies; future prospects of 25% for self-employed aged 40-50.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the framework for computing just compensation. The court applied Pranay Sethi principles: multiplier based on deceased's age (not claimants'), future prospects for self-employed, and standard deductions. This supports our quantum claim.
supporting.quote: The multiplier to be used should be as mentioned in Column (4) of the table above... which starts with an operative multiplier of 18... M-14 for 41 to 45 years.

supporting.title: No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... vs No.1 Has Filed The Written Statement To ...
supporting.principle: In fatal accident claims, when the deceased is below 40 years of age and in stable employment with regular income, 50% of actual income must be added towards future prospects. For 3 dependents, 1/3rd is deducted for personal expenses.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 32, 3 dependents. Tribunal added 50% future prospects (since deceased was below 40), deducted 1/3rd, applied multiplier of 16. Our deceased is 42 (above 40), so 25% future prospects apply, with multiplier 14.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the correct application of Sarla Verma/Pranay Sethi framework for dependency calculation. Useful as a worked example of the computation methodology.
supporting.quote: As per the principles laid down in Sarala Varma's Case, considering the number of the dependents, i.e., 3, 1/3rd of the income has to be deducted towards personal expenses of the deceased.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks and does not extend to own-damage claims or disputes between the insurer and the insured where no third party is involved. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach has limits. However, this case expressly confines its holding to 'own damage' claims (non-third-party). Since our client is a third-party claimant, this judgment actually affirms that Swaran Singh applies to her case. The insurer may try to misuse it to argue that a 'fake' or 'no licence' situation is different from a 'missing endorsement' situation.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Laxmi Narain Dhut expressly states: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks' and 'In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.' Our client is a third party. The judgment therefore supports our position, not the insurer's. The insurer cannot use it to avoid third-party liability.
adverse.quote: In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
adverse.principle: Only legal representatives who were dependent upon the victim at the time of death are entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'; non-dependent legal representatives can only claim under loss to estate.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue that the two minor children (aged 8 and 12) are dependents but may try to dispute the dependency status of the widow if she has independent income. However, on the given facts (wife and two minor children), all three are clearly dependents.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about a major son who was gainfully employed and not dependent on the deceased. Our client's dependents are a widow and two minor children (8 and 12) — all clearly dependent. The principle actually supports our client by confirming that genuine dependents are entitled to loss of dependency.
adverse.quote: A legal representative of a victim of a motor accident, who was not dependent upon the deceased, though can lay a claim for compensation, he is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
adverse.principle: When a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after its expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period. The driver does not hold a valid licence during the lapsed period, but a pay-and-recover order may be issued.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that a lapsed/no licence constitutes a breach. However, the court still ordered pay-and-recover. The risk is that the insurer will argue this establishes the breach, but the remedy remains pay-and-recover.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third party. The court held: 'Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded... the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.' This supports our position.
adverse.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. Mere non-renewal does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this for the proposition that an expired licence is a breach. However, the court held the insurer liable. This is actually favourable to our client on the liability issue.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court held the insurer jointly and severally liable with the owners despite the expired licence. It found that an expired licence (which was later renewed) does not constitute a fundamental breach. This supports the claimant's position that the insurer must pay.
adverse.quote: The insurance company is bound to satisfy the award passed against the third party and the conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous/hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving licence is mandatory. Absence thereof constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that a missing endorsement/special authorisation is a breach. However, the court still ordered pay-and-recover. The risk is low because the remedy protects the third party.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court expressly held: 'the insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.' This supports our position.
adverse.quote: The insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

priority_arguments: 1. STATUTORY LIABILITY OVERRIDES CONTRACTUAL BREACH: Lead with the principle from Satto (doc_033), S.Iyyapan (doc_032), and Yallavva (doc_025) that Section 149(1) of the MV Act imposes a statutory duty on the insurer to satisfy third-party awards regardless of policy breaches. The insurer's defence that the policy is 'void' is legally misconceived — the policy remains effective vis-à-vis third parties; the insurer's remedy is recovery from the insured.

2. PAY-AND-RECOVER IS THE ESTABLISHED REMEDY: Even if the Tribunal finds a fundamental breach (driver with no licence), the consistent line of authority (doc_024 Sunil Shreesail Killiket, doc_033 Satto, doc_035 Vijayakumar, doc_027 Chennamma) holds that the proper order is pay-and-recover, not absolving the insurer. Cite Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba (cited in doc_024) for the Supreme Court's endorsement of this principle.

3. BURDEN OF PROOF ON INSURER: The insurer must prove (a) that the driver had no licence, AND (b) that the breach was conscious and wilful on the part of the insured (owner). Mere absence of a licence does not automatically absolve the insurer — the owner's knowledge must be established. If the transport company owner was not aware or could not reasonably have known, the breach may not be 'fundamental' (see doc_033 citing Swaran Singh).

4. QUANTUM: Deceased aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, 3 dependents (wife + 2 minor children). Apply: (i) Future prospects: 25% (self-employed, age 40-50 per Pranay Sethi) → Rs 43,750/month; (ii) Deduction: 1/3rd (2-3 dependents per Sarla Verma) → Rs 29,167/month; (iii) Multiplier: 14 (age 42 per Sarla Verma table); (iv) Loss of dependency: Rs 29,167 × 12 × 14 = Rs 4,900,000; (v) Conventional heads: Rs 19,965 (loss of estate) + Rs 19,965 (funeral) + Rs 159,720 (spousal + parental consortium for 3 claimants) = Rs 199,650; (vi) TOTAL: ~Rs 51,00,000. Interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from petition date.

5. NO CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE: There is no indication the deceased contributed to the accident. If the insurer raises this, cite doc_006 (Meena) for the principle that consistent eye-witness testimony cannot be overridden by assumptions from a site plan.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51 lakh to Rs 53 lakh) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of claim petition until realisation.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework. Monthly income Rs 35,000. Age 42 → multiplier 14. Self-employed → 25% future prospects. 3 dependents → 1/3rd deduction. Loss of dependency = Rs 35,000 × 1.25 × 2/3 × 12 × 14 = Rs 4,90,0000. Conventional heads as per Pranay Sethi (Rs 19,965 each for loss of estate and funeral) and Magma General / Satinder Kaur for consortium (Rs 159,720 for 3 claimants: spouse + 2 children). Total ~Rs 51 lakh. The upper range reflects the possibility that the deceased's employment could be classified as 'permanent' (if he was in regular salaried employment with the transport company), which would attract 30% future prospects instead of 25%.
risks: The primary risk is that the Tribunal might accept the insurer's argument that a driver with NO licence at all (as opposed to an expired or missing endorsement) constitutes a more serious breach. However, the corpus consistently holds that even fundamental breach results in pay-and-recover, not absolving the insurer (doc_024, doc_025).

Risk that the owner/transport company may become insolvent or untraceable, making the insurer's recovery right illusory. This does not affect our client's right to be paid by the insurer first, but the insurer may argue this as a reason to avoid liability — though this argument has been consistently rejected by courts.

Risk that the insurer may challenge the income proof (Rs 35,000/month). Ensure salary slips, bank statements, or employer certificate are on record. If the income is not fully documented, the Tribunal may adopt a lower notional income.
Risk that the insurer may argue contributory negligence if there is any ambiguity in the accident site plan. Prepare eye-witness evidence to counter this.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim petition under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek a declaration that the insurer is liable to pay the entire awarded compensation with interest, with liberty to recover the same from the owner/driver of the offending vehicle. Alternatively, if the insurer's defence is not proved (i.e., they fail to establish conscious breach by the owner), seek direct liability without recovery rights.

caveats: The corpus does not contain any judgment where the insurer was completely absolved of third-party liability for a driver with no licence. Every relevant judgment in the corpus that addresses third-party claims orders pay-and-recover at minimum. This is consistent with the statutory scheme under Section 149 MV Act.

The corpus does not contain a judgment directly on the facts of a commercial truck driver with absolutely no licence ever issued (as opposed to expired, fake, or missing endorsement). However, doc_024 (Sunil Shreesail Killiket) comes closest — the driver had no licence at all, and the Tribunal still ordered pay-and-recover.

doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) is an insurer-favouring judgment but is expressly limited to own-damage claims and does not apply to third-party claims. It is included in adverse only because the insurer will inevitably cite it; a careful reading shows it supports our position on third-party claims.

Several judgments in the corpus (doc_002, doc_014, doc_028, doc_029, doc_038, doc_051, doc_054) are from unrelated areas of law (tractor use, gratuitous passengers, consumer disputes, criminal law, specific performance) and have no bearing on this matter.

args.question: Motor accident claim by Mrs. Lakshmi Devi (widow) for death of spouse aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, with two minor children (8 and 12). Commercial truck involved; driver had no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing policy void due to unlicensed driver. Research supporting and adverse precedents, and strategy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured. The breach must be conscious and wilful on the part of the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver held only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial). The court held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights against the owner/driver.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent. It squarely holds that even where the insurer proves a conscious breach (driver lacking proper licence for commercial vehicle), the third-party claimant is still entitled to payment from the insurer, who can then recover from the insured. This defeats the insurer's primary defence.
supporting.quote: Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings as the case may be, as ordered by the Claims Tribunal or the Court.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased was a third-party victim (cyclist) hit by a Mahindra Maxi Cab. The driver had an LMV licence but no commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable. Our case involves a commercial truck with a driver holding no licence at all — this is a stronger case for the claimant on the liability principle.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supreme Court authority that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties overrides contractual defences based on licence deficiencies. The Court emphasised that the third party's right to recover from the insurer is a statutory right that cannot be defeated by policy breaches.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment or award as a judgment debtor and recover the amount from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision holding that even fundamental breach does not absolve the insurer of liability to third parties. The only exception is fraud/collusion between the victim and insured — which is not alleged here.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench authority that comprehensively answers the insurer's argument. It holds that the 'pay and recover' principle applies irrespective of whether the policy is an Act policy or a contractual policy, and even for fundamental breaches.
supporting.quote: The Insurer is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149(2), even if it is a fundamental breach (that is breach of condition which is the cause for the accident) and the insurer proves the said breach, in view of the mandate under Section 149(1) of the Act.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, but to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all — identical to our facts. The Tribunal found a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant, citing Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba and Shamanna.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match in the corpus: a driver with no licence at all. Despite finding a fundamental breach, the Tribunal protected the third party by ordering pay-and-recover. This directly supports our client's position that she must be paid.
supporting.quote: It is admitted fact that the offending vehicle is covered with valid insurance at the time of alleged accident... the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence but no badge/authorisation for tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle). The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck with no licence at all — the principle applies a fortiori.
supporting.why_it_matters: Madras High Court confirms that even where the insurer proves breach, the proper remedy is pay-and-recover, not absolving the insurer. The court specifically held that 'the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation and recover it from the owner.'
supporting.quote: Keeping in view the nature of injuries... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent - Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV/transport endorsement but not HGV endorsement for a lorry (16,200 kg). The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our commercial truck case is analogous — the driver lacked the required licence for the vehicle class.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the driver is not licensed for the specific class of commercial vehicle, the third-party claimant is protected. The insurer must pay first and recover later.
supporting.quote: When the driver of the vehicle involved in the accident did not have a valid driving licence, whether the insurer can be directed to pay compensation to the Claimants and recover the same subsequently from the insured.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: The multiplier must be applied with reference to the age of the deceased, future prospects must be awarded even for self-employed persons based on standardised percentages, and appellate courts have power to enhance compensation.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 23, self-employed. The court applied Sarla Verma multiplier table (age-based), added future prospects, and corrected the Tribunal's errors. Our deceased is 42 — multiplier of 14 applies; future prospects of 25% for self-employed aged 40-50.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the framework for computing just compensation. The court applied Pranay Sethi principles: multiplier based on deceased's age (not claimants'), future prospects for self-employed, and standard deductions. This supports our quantum claim.
supporting.quote: The multiplier to be used should be as mentioned in Column (4) of the table above... which starts with an operative multiplier of 18... M-14 for 41 to 45 years.

supporting.title: No.4 Is A Mother Of The Deceased Sri. M. ... vs No.1 Has Filed The Written Statement To ...
supporting.principle: In fatal accident claims, when the deceased is below 40 years of age and in stable employment with regular income, 50% of actual income must be added towards future prospects. For 3 dependents, 1/3rd is deducted for personal expenses.
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased aged 32, 3 dependents. Tribunal added 50% future prospects (since deceased was below 40), deducted 1/3rd, applied multiplier of 16. Our deceased is 42 (above 40), so 25% future prospects apply, with multiplier 14.
supporting.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the correct application of Sarla Verma/Pranay Sethi framework for dependency calculation. Useful as a worked example of the computation methodology.
supporting.quote: As per the principles laid down in Sarala Varma's Case, considering the number of the dependents, i.e., 3, 1/3rd of the income has to be deducted towards personal expenses of the deceased.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner. Consistent eye-witness testimony cannot be overridden by assumptions from a site plan.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver of a tanker had no valid licence. The Tribunal found no valid licence but ordered pay-and-recover. The High Court upheld this and also set aside a finding of contributory negligence that was based only on a site plan.
supporting.why_it_matters: Directly supports our position on both liability (pay-and-recover for unlicensed driver) and quantum (no contributory negligence without evidence). The insurer's appeal was dismissed.
supporting.quote: Learned Tribunal though has accepted that there was no valid licence with the driver of the Tanker but even then has directed the insurance company to pay compensation to the claimants with a right to recover it from the owner.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Ellappa
adverse.principle: The insurance company has no statutory liability to pay compensation to passengers travelling in a goods vehicle. The 'pay and recover' doctrine is not applicable ipso facto to cases where there is no statutory requirement to cover the liability.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that the 'pay and recover' principle is not an automatic or absolute right — it applies only where the insurer had a statutory liability under Section 147 in the first place. The insurer may try to extend this logic to argue that if the vehicle was being driven in a manner fundamentally outside the policy (unlicensed driver), there is no 'statutory liability' to trigger pay-and-recover. This is a real argument that requires a careful answer.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Ellappa is about passengers in goods vehicles — a category of persons whom the MV Act does not require to be insured at all. Our client is a third-party road user (pedestrian/cyclist/other vehicle occupant), who is squarely within the class of persons whom Section 147 mandates be covered. The statutory liability under Section 147(1)(b) for death/injury to a third party is fundamentally different from the gratuitous passenger situation. Every judgment in our favour (Satto, S.Iyyapan, Yallavva, Sunil Shreesail Killiket) confirms that third-party road users are entitled to the protection of Section 149 regardless of policy breaches.
adverse.quote: Since there is no statutory requirement to cover the liability in respect of a passenger in a goods vehicle, the principle of 'pay and recover', as statutorily recognised in Section 149(4) and Section 149(5), is not applicable ipso facto to such cases.

adverse.title: Dadapeera S/O Abdul Salam Sab vs Mallesh M S/O Hanumanthappa
adverse.principle: A person travelling on the mud-guard of a tractor is not a 'third party' entitled to the benefit of pay-and-recover under Section 149, because such travel violates Regulation 28 of the Rules of the Road Regulations and is outside the scope of statutory insurance.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this for the proposition that the 'pay and recover' remedy is not available to every claimant — it is a statutory benefit available only to 'third parties' properly so-called. The insurer may argue that if the vehicle was being used in a manner that fundamentally departs from its permitted use (e.g., driven by an unlicensed driver with the owner's knowledge), the claimant is not a 'third party' entitled to the benefit. This is a distinguishable but real argument that opposing counsel will raise.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Dadapeera turned on the fact that the claimant was sitting on a tractor mud-guard — a position that is itself illegal under Regulation 28. The court held such a person cannot claim to be a 'third party' because they were participating in the illegal use of the vehicle. Our client was a completely innocent road user — a pedestrian/occupant of another vehicle — who had no involvement in the truck's operation or the driver's licensing. She is the paradigm of a 'third party' whom the MV Act was designed to protect. The court in Dadapeera itself distinguished between persons who are 'not third parties' (like the mud-guard passenger) and genuine third parties who get full statutory protection.
adverse.quote: The benefit of pay and recovery is a statutory benefit and protection given to the third party... In the present case, the claimant by sitting over mud-guard of tractor engine, cannot claim to be a third party.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured. The breach must be conscious and wilful on the part of the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver held only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial). The court held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights against the owner/driver.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent. It squarely holds that even where the insurer proves a conscious breach (driver lacking proper licence for commercial vehicle), the third-party claimant is still entitled to payment from the insurer, who can then recover from the insured. This defeats the insurer's primary defence.
supporting.quote: Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings as the case may be, as ordered by the Claims Tribunal or the Court.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased was a third-party victim (cyclist) hit by a Mahindra Maxi Cab. The driver had an LMV licence but no commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable. Our case involves a commercial truck with a driver holding no licence at all — this is a stronger case for the claimant on the liability principle.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supreme Court authority that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties overrides contractual defences based on licence deficiencies. The Court emphasised that the third party's right to recover from the insurer is a statutory right that cannot be defeated by policy breaches.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment or award as a judgment debtor and recover the amount from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision holding that even fundamental breach does not absolve the insurer of liability to third parties. The only exception is fraud/collusion between the victim and insured — which is not alleged here.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench authority that comprehensively answers the insurer's argument. It holds that the 'pay and recover' principle applies irrespective of whether the policy is an Act policy or a contractual policy, and even for fundamental breaches.
supporting.quote: The Insurer is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149(2), even if it is a fundamental breach (that is breach of condition which is the cause for the accident) and the insurer proves the said breach, in view of the mandate under Section 149(1) of the Act.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, but to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all — identical to our facts. The Tribunal found a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant, citing Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba and Shamanna.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match in the corpus: a driver with no licence at all. Despite finding a fundamental breach, the Tribunal protected the third party by ordering pay-and-recover. This directly supports our client's position that she must be paid.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV licence but no badge/authorisation for tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle). The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our case involves a commercial truck with no licence at all — the principle applies a fortiori.
supporting.why_it_matters: Madras High Court confirms that even where the insurer proves breach, the proper remedy is pay-and-recover, not absolving the insurer. The court specifically held that 'the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation and recover it from the owner.'

supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV/transport endorsement but not HGV endorsement for a lorry (16,200 kg). The court ordered pay-and-recover. Our commercial truck case is analogous — the driver lacked the required licence for the vehicle class.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the driver is not licensed for the specific class of commercial vehicle, the third-party claimant is protected. The insurer must pay first and recover later.

However, the corpus consistently holds that even fundamental breach results in pay-and-recover, not absolving the insurer (doc_024, doc_025).

Risk that the owner/transport company may become insolvent or untraceable, making the insurer's recovery right illusory. This does not affect our client's right to be paid by the insurer first, but the insurer may argue this as a reason to avoid liability — though this argument has been consistently rejected by courts.

Risk that the insurer may challenge the income proof (Rs 35,000/month). Ensure salary slips, bank statements, or employer certificate are on record. If the income is not fully documented, the Tribunal may adopt a lower notional income.
Risk that the insurer may argue contributory negligence if there is any ambiguity in the accident site plan. Prepare eye-witness evidence to counter this.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim petition under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek a declaration that the insurer is liable to pay the entire awarded compensation with interest, with liberty to recover the same from the owner/driver of the offending vehicle. Alternatively, if the insurer's defence is not proved (i.e., they fail to establish conscious breach by the owner), seek direct liability without recovery rights.

caveats: doc_016 (Reserved On: 21.07.2025 vs State Of H.P) — Criminal revision about rash driving conviction under IPC and Section 181 MV Act. The court set aside the IPC convictions but upheld the fine under Section 181 for driving without a licence. This is a criminal case with no bearing on civil compensation liability of the insurer to third parties. The court expressly held that absence of a licence does not prove negligence in driving. Not relevant to our client's claim.
